Oracle rethinks modular Java plan after Red Hat's objections
Jdk 9!! Fuck I'm way behind I'm still on 7

I'm astonished, considering that the cited message from Oracle is full of contradictory statements and also not really good language.

Unluckily, I don't know too much about what they are discussing to have much of an opinion.

In general terms, you obviously want to know where you got your routines from, if you use ready-made routines from other sources. Just downloading something, with random names, where many repositories may use the same names, would be quite annoying. Finding a bug and having difficulties to determine which source the code comes from, would also not be practical. And that also implies that you use names specific to you or your company so that if you publicise something, the others won't run into such issues.

It seems Oracle wants to make sure names include group, project name, and version, but is geared towards a simple approach for small devices where the names of routines inside a repository may conflict with other names in other repositories, and leave it to the programmers to fix those. While the programmers (RedHat), want all names to be modular (isolated from other modules) so that its easier for instance to use modules of other companies at run-time, and without changing them with every update.

Oracle is quite aware of the manual tweaking required with their approach, but is reluctant to go into a direction where all needs to be perfectly modular, leading to performance issues, to complex code which might requires more memory, which might exceed the budget of a microwave or the size constraints of a smart watch.

I think it shows the limits of trying to make the same java work for anything from a small sensor to a large project spread out to several servers.

If I had any say, I'd create different levels of joining modules:

1) A very primitive level, mostly for smaller devices and quickly and easily adding a module where not too many changes are needed to make it work, and where the finished program won't need to load the modules from an untested source (all is always updated together).

2) A standard level, with as much modularisation as possible without causing big programming, performance, or resource usage headaches.

3) A high level, where full modularisation, and other 'ideal' (meta) adaptions are implemented, to allow more things (runtime options, backwards- and forward compatibility of modules and the data they exchange, and so on). No regards to resource use or speed, and all good solutions may find their way into the lower level(s) eventually. No guarantees that using those methods will work on embedded devices or such.

4) An experimental level, where new ideas can be tested and criticised, but all can change with the next update of Java - no guarantees for any functionality.
